stem: Each of the students ______ a laptop for the course.
explanation: 'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb because the subject is 'each', not 'students'. So 'Each of the students has'. 'Have' is tempting because 'students' stands next to the verb, but it is only the object of 'of'.

stem: Identify the error: The box of old letters (A) were found (B) in the attic (C) by my grandmother (D) last week.
explanation: The subject is 'The box', which is singular; 'of old letters' only describes it. The verb must agree with the head noun: 'The box ... was found'. The other parts are correct: 'in the attic', 'by my grandmother' (passive agent) and 'last week' with the past tense.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Neither the manager nor his assistants was present at the meeting.
The quality of these mangoes are excellent this year.
Either the students or the teacher is responsible for the noise.
The pictures on the wall was painted by my aunt.
explanation: With 'either ... or' and 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'the teacher is'. In the first sentence the nearer subject 'his assistants' is plural, so it needs 'were'. 'The quality ... is' and 'The pictures ... were' follow the head noun, not the noun in the 'of' or 'on' phrase.

stem: Mathematics ______ my favourite subject since Class 6.
explanation: Subjects ending in -ics, such as mathematics and physics, are singular, and 'since Class 6' needs the present perfect. So 'Mathematics has been'. 'Have been' has the right tense but treats 'mathematics' as plural because of the final -s.

stem: Identify the error: The teacher, (A) along with her students, (B) are planning (C) a visit (D) to the museum.
explanation: Phrases such as 'along with', 'as well as' and 'together with' do not change the number of the subject. The subject is 'The teacher', so the verb must be 'is planning'. The plural 'students' inside the commas misleads many readers into choosing 'are'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: There is many books on the shelf.
There are a lot of traffic on the road today.
There is a lot of traffic on the road today.
There are a little milk left in the jug.
explanation: After 'there is/are' the verb agrees with the noun that follows. 'Traffic' and 'milk' are uncountable and take 'is', while 'books' is plural and takes 'are'. 'A lot of' does not make 'traffic' plural, so 'There are a lot of traffic' is wrong.

stem: Bread and butter ______ his usual breakfast.
explanation: Two nouns joined by 'and' normally take a plural verb, but when they name a single idea or dish, as in 'bread and butter', the verb is singular. Here they form one breakfast, so 'is'. 'Are' applies the general 'and' rule without noticing that the pair is one item.

stem: Identify the error: A number of candidates (A) has applied (B) for the post, but (C) only a few (D) will be selected.
explanation: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb: 'A number of candidates have applied'. Do not confuse it with 'The number of', which takes a singular verb ('The number of candidates is large'). 'Only a few' correctly means 'some, but not many'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The number of road accidents have risen sharply.
The scissors is on the table next to the thread.
The news from the flooded villages is worrying.
explanation: 'News' is uncountable and always singular, so 'The news ... is' is correct. 'The number of' takes a singular verb ('has risen'), 'mathematics' is singular, and 'scissors' is a plural-only noun that takes 'are'.

stem: The police ______ looking into the matter.
explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun in standard English, like 'cattle' and 'people', so it takes a plural verb: 'The police are looking'. 'Is' and 'was' treat it as a singular group noun, which is a common mistake.

stem: Identify the error: Every year many a student (A) from small towns (B) dream (C) of studying (D) at NUST.
explanation: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: 'many a student dreams'. 'From small towns' only describes the student. 'Dream of + -ing' and 'at NUST' are correct.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Physics and chemistry is compulsory for us.
Every boy and girl were given a prize.
The teacher and the students was in the hall.
The boy and his sister have gone to Multan.
explanation: Two different people or things joined by 'and' take a plural verb, so 'The boy and his sister have gone' is correct, and the first and third sentences should use 'are' and 'were'. When 'every' or 'each' comes before nouns joined by 'and', the verb is singular: 'Every boy and girl was given a prize'.

stem: Identify the error: The judges (A) were impressed, and (B) the prize (C) was shared between Ayesha (D) and I.
explanation: A pronoun that is the object of a preposition takes the object case. 'Between' is a preposition, so it must be 'between Ayesha and me'. Test it by removing 'Ayesha and': nobody would say 'between I'.

stem: The children enjoyed ______ at the picnic.
explanation: The reflexive pronoun for 'they' is 'themselves', used when the object is the same as the subject. 'Theirselves' and 'themself' are non-standard forms, and 'themselfs' misspells the plural of 'self' (selves).

stem: This bag is not mine; it must be ______.
explanation: A possessive pronoun that stands alone, without a noun after it, is 'hers' (like 'mine', 'yours', 'ours'). Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe, so 'her's' is wrong; 'she's' means 'she is', and 'her' needs a noun after it ('her bag').

stem: Identify the error: The company (A) has decided (B) to move (C) it's head office (D) to Lahore.
explanation: 'It's' is the short form of 'it is' or 'it has'; the possessive pronoun is 'its', with no apostrophe. The sentence needs 'its head office'. 'Has decided' agrees with the singular 'The company'.

stem: The officer to ______ you should send the form is on leave.
explanation: A relative pronoun directly after a preposition takes the object form, so 'to whom'. 'Who' is the subject form and cannot follow 'to'. 'Which' is used for things, not people, and 'whose' needs a noun after it.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We students want a longer break.
The coach gave Hamza and I extra practice.
Him and his brother run a shop in Saddar.
Fatima and myself will host the event.
explanation: 'We' is the subject form, so 'We students want' is correct (test by dropping 'students': 'We want'). 'Gave Hamza and I' needs the object form 'me', 'Him and his brother' as a subject needs 'He', and a reflexive pronoun cannot be a subject, so 'Fatima and I will host'.

stem: I met the doctor ______ son is in my class.
explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun: the son belongs to the doctor ('the doctor whose son'). 'Who' and 'whom' cannot be followed directly by the noun 'son' in this way, and 'which' refers to things.

stem: Identify the error: My brother and (A) me (B) went (C) to the market (D) yesterday.
explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject, so it needs the subject case: 'My brother and I went'. Remove 'My brother and' to test it: 'me went' is clearly wrong. 'Went' correctly matches 'yesterday'.

stem: He has lived in Peshawar ______ 2019.
explanation: With the present perfect, 'since' is used before a point in time (2019, Monday, March) and 'for' before a length of time (five years). 2019 is a point in time, so 'since'. 'In 2019' would need the simple past ('He moved there in 2019').

stem: Identify the error: I (A) have watched (B) that film (C) with my friends (D) at the cinema last Friday.
explanation: The present perfect is not used with a finished past time such as 'last Friday', 'yesterday' or 'two days ago'. The simple past is needed: 'I watched that film'. 'With my friends' and 'at the cinema' are correct prepositions.

stem: By the time we reached the station, the train ______.
explanation: When one past action was complete before another past action, the earlier one takes the past perfect. The train left before we reached the station, so 'had already left'. 'Has already left' is present perfect and does not fit a story told in the past ('reached').

stem: Identify the error: She (A) is knowing (B) the answer, but (C) she is too shy (D) to speak.
explanation: Stative verbs such as know, believe, understand, own and like are not normally used in the continuous tenses. The sentence needs the simple present: 'She knows the answer'. 'Too shy to speak' is the correct 'too + adjective + to-infinitive' pattern.

stem: Look at those dark clouds! It ______ rain.
explanation: 'Be going to' is used for a prediction based on present evidence, here the dark clouds. So 'It is going to rain'. 'Goes to' and 'is raining to' are not English future forms, and 'will be going rain' is ungrammatical.

stem: I will call you when I ______ in Karachi.
explanation: In a time clause beginning with when, as soon as, until, before or after, the simple present is used for a future action; 'will' goes only in the main clause. So 'I will call you when I arrive'. 'When I will arrive' puts the future in the time clause, which is wrong.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am living in Quetta since 2020.
The bus left before we have arrived.
She has been working at the bank for six years.
He has finished the report two hours ago.
explanation: An action that began in the past and still continues takes the present perfect continuous with 'for' or 'since': 'has been working ... for six years'. 'Am living ... since 2020' should be 'have been living', and 'two hours ago' marks a finished past time, so it needs the simple past 'finished'. 'Before we have arrived' should be 'before we arrived'.

stem: No sooner had the bell rung ______ the students rushed out.
explanation: The fixed pattern is 'No sooner + had + subject + past participle ... than + simple past'. So 'No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out'. 'When' belongs with 'hardly' and 'scarcely', which is why it is the most tempting wrong choice.

stem: Hardly ______ the hall when the lights went out.
explanation: When a sentence begins with the negative adverb 'Hardly', the subject and auxiliary are inverted, and the earlier action takes the past perfect: 'Hardly had we entered the hall when ...'. 'We had entered' keeps normal word order, and 'did we entered' wrongly uses a past form after 'did'.

stem: Identify the error: It (A) has been (B) raining (C) since three hours, (D) so the roads are flooded.
explanation: 'Three hours' is a length of time, so it takes 'for', not 'since': 'It has been raining for three hours'. 'Since' is used only before a starting point, such as 'since morning' or 'since 6 o'clock'. The present perfect continuous 'has been raining' is correct.

stem: While I ______ for the exam, the power went off.
explanation: A longer action in progress in the past that is interrupted by a short past action takes the past continuous: 'While I was studying ..., the power went off'. 'Am studying' is present and clashes with 'went off', and 'has been studying' does not agree with 'I'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Water boil at 100 °C at sea level.
The earth moves round the sun.
The sun is rising in the east every day.
Birds is flying south in winter.
explanation: Facts and general truths take the simple present, with -s for a singular subject: 'The earth moves'. 'Water boil' lacks the -s, and 'is rising ... every day' uses the continuous for a permanent truth. 'Birds is flying' breaks agreement and uses the wrong tense.

stem: Identify the error: When I (A) reached the hall, I (B) realised that I (C) left my admit card (D) at home.
explanation: Leaving the card happened before reaching the hall and realising, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect: 'I had left my admit card at home'. 'Reached' and 'realised' are both simple past because they happen in sequence at the same point in the story.

stem: Ayesha ______ her homework yet.
explanation: In British English, 'yet' in a negative sentence goes with the present perfect, because it means 'up to now': 'has not finished ... yet'. 'Did not finish' is simple past and refers to a finished time, which does not fit 'yet'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He go to college by bus every day.
They was playing hockey when it began to rain.
We have known each other since childhood.
explanation: The present perfect with 'since' shows a state that began in the past and continues, and 'have' agrees with 'We'. 'He go' needs 'goes' for a singular subject, 'They was' needs 'were', and 'She have' needs 'has'.

stem: Identify the error: Every morning my father (A) is reading (B) the newspaper (C) before he (D) leaves for work.
explanation: A habit or routine, signalled by 'every morning', takes the simple present: 'my father reads the newspaper'. The present continuous is for actions happening now. 'Leaves' is correctly simple present in the time clause.

stem: It is high time we ______ the old wiring in this building.
explanation: After 'It is (high) time + subject', the verb is in the past tense even though the meaning is present or future: 'It is high time we replaced'. The past form shows that the action is overdue. 'Replace' looks natural because the meaning is present, but it breaks this fixed pattern.

stem: She ______ in this school for ten years when she retired last year.
explanation: The ten years of teaching came before another past point (her retirement), so the past perfect is needed: 'She had taught ... for ten years when she retired'. 'Has taught' is present perfect, which cannot be tied to a past event such as 'last year'.

stem: Identify the error: Hamza (A) did not (B) went (C) to the match because he (D) was ill.
explanation: After the auxiliary 'did' (and 'does', 'do'), the main verb is in the base form: 'did not go'. The past tense is already shown by 'did', so 'went' doubles it. 'Was ill' agrees with 'he' and is in the past tense.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am waiting here for two hours.
The film had started before we will reach.
We has visited the museum twice.
She was cooking when the guests arrived.
explanation: An action in progress (was cooking) interrupted by a short past action (arrived) takes the past continuous plus the simple past. 'I am waiting ... for two hours' needs 'I have been waiting', 'We has' needs 'have', and the second sentence wrongly mixes the past perfect with 'will'.

stem: In which sentence does every pronoun refer clearly to only one noun?
options: Ayesha told her sister that she had won the prize.
The teacher spoke to Usman, and he thanked him.
Hamza dropped the glass on the tile, and it cracked.
Bilal thanked his teachers, who had helped him.
explanation: A pronoun must have one clear antecedent. In the last sentence 'who' can only mean the teachers and 'him' can only mean Bilal. In the others 'she' could be Ayesha or her sister, 'he' and 'him' could be either the teacher or Usman, and 'it' could be the glass or the tile.

stem: Identify the error: Since the new manager (A) took over, sales (B) are rising (C) steadily and complaints (D) have fallen.
explanation: When a 'since' clause gives the starting point of a change that continues to now, the main verb takes a perfect tense: 'sales have been rising' (or 'have risen'). 'Took over' is correctly simple past inside the 'since' clause, and 'have fallen' already follows the rule.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: When he will come, I will give him the book.
She will phone you after she will finish work.
We will start as soon as the guests will arrive.
I will wait here until you return.
explanation: In time clauses introduced by when, after, as soon as and until, the simple present is used for the future: 'until you return'. The other three wrongly put 'will' inside the time clause; they should read 'When he comes', 'after she finishes' and 'as soon as the guests arrive'.

stem: My little brother is very fond ______ reading comics.
explanation: The adjective 'fond' is always followed by 'of': 'fond of reading'. Learners often write 'fond with' or 'fond about' by analogy with 'pleased with' or 'excited about', but those prepositions do not go with 'fond'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We will meet in Sunday morning.
explanation: Prepositions of time: 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on Sunday morning), 'in' for months, years and parts of the day (in March), 'at' for clock times (at 9 o'clock). So only 'The exam is on Monday' is correct; the others need 'on Sunday morning', 'in March' and 'at 9 o'clock'.

stem: Identify the error: We (A) discussed (B) about the problem (C) for an hour but (D) reached no decision.
explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object with no preposition: 'We discussed the problem'. 'About' is used with the noun ('a discussion about') but not with the verb. 'For an hour' and 'reached no decision' are correct.

stem: This mobile phone is superior ______ that one.
explanation: Latin comparatives such as superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior and preferable are followed by 'to', not 'than': 'superior to that one'. 'Than' is tempting because 'superior' means 'better', but it is used only with -er and 'more' comparatives.

stem: He was accused ______ stealing the documents.
explanation: The verb 'accuse' takes 'of': 'accused of stealing'. 'With' goes with 'charge' ('charged with theft'), and 'for' is used with 'blame' or 'punish' ('punished for stealing'), which is why they are easy to confuse.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Our team consists of ten girls.
He entered into the room quietly.
We reached to Lahore at noon.
explanation: 'Consist' is followed by 'of': 'consists of ten girls'. 'Prefer' takes 'to' (prefers tea to coffee), and 'enter' (a room) and 'reach' (a place) take a direct object with no preposition: 'entered the room', 'reached Lahore'.

stem: Identify the error: Bilal (A) is married (B) with a doctor (C) who works (D) at a hospital in Rawalpindi.
explanation: The adjective 'married' is followed by 'to', not 'with': 'Bilal is married to a doctor'. 'Who works' is the correct relative pronoun for a person with a singular verb, and 'at a hospital' is correct.

stem: My grandmother is afraid ______ dogs.
explanation: The adjective 'afraid' is followed by 'of': 'afraid of dogs'. 'Afraid from' is a common error made by translating directly from Urdu ('se darna'), but English uses 'of' here.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: It all depends of the weather.
She was absent in the class yesterday.
We should comply with the rules.
She is not familiar about this area.
explanation: 'Comply' is followed by 'with': 'comply with the rules'. The others need 'depends on', 'absent from (the) class' and 'familiar with this area'; each wrong sentence uses a preposition that does not go with that verb or adjective.

stem: He has been charged ______ murder.
explanation: In the legal sense, a person is 'charged with' a crime: 'charged with murder'. 'Of' goes with 'accused' (accused of murder) and 'guilty' (guilty of murder), which is why it is tempting. 'Charged for' refers to paying money for something.

stem: Identify the error: (A) Despite of the heavy rain, (B) the match continued, and the crowd (C) stayed (D) until the end.
explanation: 'Despite' is a preposition on its own and is never followed by 'of': 'Despite the heavy rain'. The phrase 'in spite of' does take 'of', and mixing the two produces 'despite of'. 'Until the end' is correct.

stem: I am looking forward ______ you next month.
explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not the base verb: 'looking forward to seeing you'. 'To see' is the most tempting choice because 'to' is usually part of an infinitive.

stem: The doctor advised him to abstain ______ sugary drinks.
explanation: The verb 'abstain' is followed by 'from', like 'refrain from' and 'keep away from': 'abstain from sugary drinks'. 'Off' is used in the informal phrasal verb 'keep off', and 'against' goes with 'advise against', which is why they may seem possible.

stem: Identify the error: Although we (A) offered, Sana (B) insisted to pay (C) for (D) the whole meal.
explanation: 'Insist' is followed by 'on' + -ing, not by a to-infinitive: 'Sana insisted on paying'. 'Pay for' (the meal) is correct. Learners confuse 'insist' with verbs such as 'want' and 'decide', which do take 'to'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She came to college by foot.
He arrived to Lahore at night.
We went to Islamabad by train.
They travelled in bus to Multan.
explanation: Means of transport take 'by' with no article: 'by train', 'by bus', 'by car'. The exception is walking, which is 'on foot', not 'by foot'. 'Arrive' takes 'in' for a city or country ('arrived in Lahore'), never 'to'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He is senior than me in the office.
She is responsible of the accounts.
I am capable to solve this problem.
explanation: 'Interested' is followed by 'in'. The others need 'senior to' (Latin comparatives take 'to'), 'responsible for' and 'capable of solving'; 'capable' is never followed by a to-infinitive.

stem: The novel was translated ______ Urdu last year.
explanation: A text is translated 'into' another language, because the preposition shows change from one form to another, as in 'convert into' and 'change into'. 'Onto' shows movement to a surface, and 'at' and 'with' do not combine with 'translate' in this sense.

stem: She has been suffering ______ fever since Tuesday.
explanation: The verb 'suffer' takes 'from' before an illness or problem: 'suffering from fever'. 'Suffering of' is a common error, perhaps by analogy with 'die of', but 'suffer' does not take 'of'.

stem: Identify the error: The new rule (A) prevents students (B) to use (C) their phones (D) during lectures.
explanation: 'Prevent' follows the pattern 'prevent somebody from doing something': 'prevents students from using their phones'. A to-infinitive cannot follow 'prevent'. 'Prevents' agrees with the singular 'rule', and 'during lectures' is correct.

stem: Identify the error: Zainab's parents (A) were (B) delighted, and (C) she was proud (D) for her brother's success.
explanation: The adjective 'proud' is followed by 'of': 'proud of her brother's success'. 'Were' agrees with the plural 'parents', and 'she was proud' is correct. 'For' is used with 'happy for' someone, which is why it slips in here.

stem: Ali was born ______ 2008.
explanation: Years, months and seasons take 'in': 'born in 2008', 'in March', 'in winter'. 'On' is for days and full dates (born on 5 May 2008), and 'at' is for clock times, so neither fits a year on its own.

stem: It took us ______ hour to reach Murree.
explanation: The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on the first sound, not the first letter. In 'hour' the h is silent and the word begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an': 'an hour'. 'A hour' follows the spelling rather than the sound.

stem: Identify the error: He (A) hopes to (B) join (C) an university (D) abroad.
explanation: 'University' begins with a 'you' sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes 'a': 'a university', like 'a uniform' and 'a European'. 'An' is used only before a vowel sound. 'Hopes to join' and 'abroad' are correct.

stem: ______ Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
explanation: Names of rivers, seas, oceans and deserts take the definite article: 'the Indus', 'the Arabian Sea', 'the Thar'. The superlative 'the longest' also shows that one particular thing is meant, so 'a' and 'an' are wrong.

stem: Identify the error: (A) The Mount Everest is (B) the highest (C) peak in (D) the world.
explanation: Names of single mountains take no article: 'Mount Everest', 'K2', 'Nanga Parbat'. Mountain ranges do take 'the' (the Himalayas, the Karakoram). 'The highest' (superlative) and 'the world' (unique thing) correctly use 'the'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He gave me many advices before the exam.
He bought a new furniture for his room.
Can you give me some information?
I need a informations about the hostel.
explanation: Advice, furniture and information are uncountable nouns: they have no plural and do not take 'a' or 'an'. 'Some information' is correct. To count them, use 'a piece of advice' or 'an item of furniture'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He gave me an useful tip.
explanation: 'One' begins with a 'w' sound, a consonant sound, so 'a one-eyed cat' is correct. 'European' and 'useful' begin with a 'you' sound and take 'a', while 'honest' begins with a vowel sound (silent h) and takes 'an'. The rule depends on sound, not spelling.

stem: Identify the error: The technician (A) took (B) a X-ray (C) of my (D) wrist.
explanation: The letter X is pronounced 'eks', which begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an': 'an X-ray', like 'an MBA' and 'an FIR'. The article follows the sound of the first letter, not whether it is written as a consonant.

stem: Identify the error: Sana (A) is (B) tallest girl (C) in (D) our class.
explanation: A superlative adjective before a noun takes the definite article, because it picks out one particular person: 'the tallest girl in our class'. 'In our class' is the correct preposition after a superlative, and 'is' agrees with 'Sana'.

stem: ______ Himalayas stretch across several countries.
explanation: Mountain ranges, like groups of islands, take 'the': 'the Himalayas', 'the Karakoram', 'the Alps'. 'A' and 'an' cannot go with a plural noun, and 'some' cannot come before a proper name.

stem: He was ______ honest man that everyone trusted him.
explanation: Before an adjective + singular countable noun, use 'such a/an', with the article chosen by sound: 'honest' has a silent h, so 'such an honest man'. 'So' is used before an adjective alone ('so honest that'), and 'such a' ignores the vowel sound.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The nature is at its best in spring.
The United States has fifty states.
She is a doctor and her husband is engineer.
She is learning the English at an institute.
explanation: Country names that contain words like 'States', 'Kingdom' or 'Republic' take 'the', and the name is treated as one country with a singular verb. 'Nature' in the general sense and names of languages ('English') take no article, and a singular job noun needs 'a' or 'an': 'an engineer'.

stem: Identify the error: We (A) are having (B) such (C) a lovely weather (D) in Murree this week.
explanation: 'Weather' is an uncountable noun, so it cannot take 'a' or 'an', even after 'such' or 'what': 'such lovely weather'. 'Are having' is correct, since 'have' here means 'experience' and can be continuous. 'In Murree' is the right preposition for a town.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The honesty is the best policy.
She plays the cricket every evening.
He went to the bed early last night.
We had dinner at a small café.
explanation: Meals in general take no article ('had dinner'), and 'a small café' is a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time. Abstract nouns used in a general sense (honesty), names of sports (cricket) and the fixed phrase 'go to bed' take no article.

stem: Hamza was ______ first person to reach the summit.
explanation: Ordinal numbers such as first, second and last pick out one particular person or thing, so they take the definite article: 'the first person'. 'A first person' and 'one first person' are not used in this sense.

stem: Identify the error: Last night (A) the stars were hidden, but (B) moon (C) was (D) unusually bright.
explanation: Things that are unique in our world, such as the sun, the moon and the sky, take the definite article: 'but the moon was unusually bright'. 'The stars were' correctly uses a plural verb, and 'unusually' is the adverb modifying 'bright'.

stem: Identify the error: (A) The Karakoram Highway links Pakistan (B) with (C) the China (D) through the Khunjerab Pass.
explanation: Most country names take no article: 'Pakistan', 'China', 'Iran'. Only names with words such as 'States', 'Kingdom' or 'Republic', or plural names, take 'the'. Named highways and passes, such as 'the Karakoram Highway' and 'the Khunjerab Pass', do take 'the'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The cattle is grazing in the field.
There is many reasons for his success.
Measles is a highly infectious disease.
explanation: Names of diseases ending in -s, such as measles and mumps, are singular: 'Measles is'. 'Cattle' is always plural ('are grazing'), 'trousers' is a plural-only noun ('need ironing'), and after 'there' the verb agrees with 'many reasons' ('There are').

stem: Identify the error: The results (A) of the survey (B) shows that most (C) students (D) prefer online classes.
explanation: The subject is the plural 'The results'; 'of the survey' only describes it. So the verb must be plural: 'The results ... show'. The singular 'survey' just before the verb makes 'shows' look right. 'Most students prefer' correctly agrees.

stem: Either Ali or his sisters ______ going to pick you up.
explanation: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. 'His sisters' is plural and next to the verb, so 'are going'. 'Is' would be correct only if the order were reversed: 'Either his sisters or Ali is going'.

stem: Identify the error: Neither (A) the players nor (B) the coach (C) were happy (D) with the referee's decision.
explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here 'the coach' is singular and nearer, so the verb should be 'was happy'. The plural 'players' at the start makes 'were' seem right. 'Happy with' a decision is the correct preposition.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: One of my friends live in Canada.
Each of the rooms have a fan.
The list of names are on the notice board.
explanation: Indefinite pronouns such as everybody, everyone and nobody take a singular verb: 'Everybody likes'. 'One of ...', 'Each of ...' and 'The list of ...' also have singular subjects (one, each, list), so they need 'lives', 'has' and 'is'.

stem: ______ turn is it to read the next paragraph?
explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive question word, used before a noun: 'Whose turn is it?' 'Who's' is the short form of 'who is' or 'who has', so it cannot come before 'turn'; 'who' and 'whom' cannot show possession.

stem: Identify the error: Please (A) send (B) the final report (C) to Bilal or (D) myself by Friday.
explanation: A reflexive pronoun such as 'myself' is used only when it refers back to the subject of the same clause (I hurt myself) or for emphasis. Here the subject is the understood 'you', so the object form is needed: 'to Bilal or me'. Using 'myself' to sound polite is a common error.

stem: ______ and I have known each other since school.
explanation: Pronouns that form part of the subject take the subject case: 'She and I have known'. Drop 'and I' to test it: 'She has known', not 'Her has known'. 'Hers' is a possessive and 'Herself' a reflexive, and neither can be a subject.

stem: Identify the error: (A) Us engineers (B) must (C) always check (D) our calculations twice.
explanation: When a pronoun comes before a noun in the subject, it takes the subject case: 'We engineers must'. Test by removing the noun: 'We must check', not 'Us must check'. 'Our calculations' is the correct possessive.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The boy which won the race is my cousin.
This is the house that my grandfather built.
The teacher whom gave us the test was strict.
Is this the pen who you lost?
explanation: 'That' can be used as a relative pronoun for things (and people), so 'the house that my grandfather built' is correct. 'Which' is for things, not people ('The boy who won'), 'who' is for people, not things ('the pen that/which you lost'), and 'whom' cannot be the subject of 'gave'.

stem: The principal invited Fatima and ______ to the ceremony.
explanation: The pronoun is part of the object of 'invited', so it takes the object case: 'invited Fatima and me'. Drop 'Fatima and' to test it: 'invited me', not 'invited I'. 'Myself' is reflexive and needs 'I' as the subject of the clause.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The number of girls has doubled.
Every one of the books were damaged in the flood.
The children has gone to bed early.
She come home late every night.
explanation: 'The number of' + plural noun takes a singular verb, because the subject is 'number': 'The number of girls has doubled'. 'Every one of' is also singular ('was damaged'), 'children' is plural ('have gone'), and 'She' needs 'comes'.

stem: Identify the error: The children (A) were playing (B) cricket when (C) it starts (D) to rain.
explanation: The tenses in a past narrative must be consistent. A past action in progress (were playing) interrupted by a short action takes the simple past for the interruption: 'when it started to rain'. 'Starts' wrongly switches to the present.

stem: She is jealous ______ her sister's success.
explanation: The adjective 'jealous' is followed by 'of', like 'envious of' and 'proud of': 'jealous of her sister's success'. 'From' is a direct translation from Urdu ('se jalna') and is not used with 'jealous' in English.

stem: Identify the error: Usman (A) has (B) a good (C) command (D) on English.
explanation: In the sense of knowing a language or skill well, 'command' is followed by 'of': 'a good command of English'. 'A good command' correctly uses 'a' with this countable use of the noun. 'On' is a common error by analogy with 'hold on' or 'control over'.

stem: She has been working on the project ______ the past three months.
explanation: 'The past three months' is a length of time, so it takes 'for' with the present perfect continuous. 'Since' is used only with a starting point ('since May'). 'From' needs a matching 'to' or 'until' and cannot introduce a period like this.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He is studying the medicine in Karachi.
He travels to work by the bus.
I have lived here for a decade.
explanation: 'A decade' is a singular countable noun naming a length of time, so 'for a decade' is correct. Academic subjects in general take no article ('studying medicine'), 'by + transport' takes no article ('by bus'), and 'umbrella' begins with a vowel sound, so 'an umbrella'.

stem: Identify the error: The rich (A) is not always (B) happy, and the poor (C) are not always (D) miserable.
explanation: 'The + adjective' used for a group of people (the rich, the poor, the young) is plural and takes a plural verb: 'The rich are not always happy'. The sentence itself shows the right form in 'the poor are'. 'Happy' and 'miserable' are adjectives after the verb 'be'.

stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Sana has went to Skardu twice.
Sana is visiting Skardu twice so far.
Sana had visited Skardu twice so far.
Sana has been to Skardu twice so far.
explanation: Experiences up to now, with 'so far', 'ever' or a number of times, take the present perfect: 'has been to Skardu twice'. 'Has went' uses the past tense instead of the past participle 'gone', and 'had visited' (past perfect) does not fit 'so far', which means 'up to now'.

stem: Identify the error: Scarcely (A) had the guests (B) sat down (C) than the (D) food arrived.
explanation: 'Scarcely' and 'hardly' are followed by 'when' (or 'before'), not 'than': 'Scarcely had the guests sat down when the food arrived'. 'Than' belongs only with 'no sooner'. 'Had the guests sat' correctly inverts the subject and auxiliary after a negative adverb.
